executive_summary: AUD/USD closed at 0.70331 on 30 October 2026. That is US dollars per Australian dollar, so a rising pair means a stronger AUD. The pair is up 1.47% over one month, down 0.19% over three months and down 2.41% over six, which puts it at the 72nd percentile of its 52-week closing range of 0.64551-0.72584. The October rebound from the 15 October intraday low of 0.68956 was driven by rates: markets went from doubting a 3 November RBA hike to largely pricing it. A hike to 4.85% would widen the gap over the Fed's 3.875% mid-point from 72.5bp to 97.5bp, and the Fed's next chance to respond is 9 December. Neither standalone view shows the standoff that appears in the pair. The AUD view leans bullish on the hike and the USD view is Bullish on growth and funding, but in the pair the two rate tailwinds largely cancel. What remains is a composite-PMI gap of almost 10 points (US 57.6, Australia 47.7) and tightening year-end dollar liquidity, both leaning against the pair, against an extreme AUD short (legacy non-commercial net -128,300 contracts) that cushions it. The tactical stance is Neutral, conviction 2, on a weighted score of -0.0262. The strategic stance is Neutral, conviction 2, at +0.0069. The chart is coiled: spot sits on the 100-day average (0.70335), just below the 200-day (0.70577) and 50-day (0.70668), and 21 pips under the 0.7054-0.7111 resistance band. Carry is only 0.10 of three-month implied volatility, and the forward and our probability-weighted path are within 7 pips of each other at every tenor, so there is no forward-mispricing trade. The plan depends on events: fade the edges of the 0.6920-0.7111 range, and switch to a directional position only on a daily close above 0.7111 or below 0.6870 that the RBA's guidance and the first-week US data confirm. Two caveats: the strategic call rests on one low-confidence rates judgement (without it the score would be Bearish at about -0.11), and the crowded short makes upside surprises sharper than downside ones.

market_context.valuation_assessment: On GDP-based PPP, AUD/USD's fair value is about 0.7148, so spot is 1.6% (115 pips) below parity. At the pair level PPP gives no signal. The real effective rates tell a sharper story. The BIS real broad index for AUD was 116.13 in September 2026, the 97th percentile of the 33 monthly readings since January 2024 and 8.77 points higher than a year earlier. The USD index was 107.11, the 21st percentile of the same window and 0.38 points lower over the year. The real-rate gap has therefore moved about 9 points in AUD's favour in twelve months. AUD's real appreciation has come from carry, during a year in which its export prices fell, while the dollar has cheapened in real terms because US inflation has outrun its partners'. At 0.70331 the pair prices the rate advantage and neither real-rate extreme. It does not price the iron-ore and oil terms-of-trade loss, and it does not price the dollar's real cheapness, so the two valuation arguments largely offset.

market_context.recent_regime: Since July AUD/USD has traded between daily lows of 0.6883 and highs of 0.7238. September's 4% slide reflected the Fed's hike and dollar strength. The October recovery came almost entirely from RBA repricing: Deputy Governor Hauser's warning and the 4.3% September CPI took 3 November hike odds from about 20% to the high 80s, and traders raised the probability of a November hike to 88% from 60% before the inflation report. The pair rose while iron ore printed a two-year low and Brent traded above US$110, so rates have temporarily overridden the terms-of-trade channel. Volatility has compressed around the converged averages ahead of the early-November cluster of events. The pair peaked in May (best close 0.72584 on 13 May), fell to a closing low of 0.68869 on 29 June, recovered to 0.72193 on 7 September, then lost 3.98% between the 9 September close of 0.72185 and the 1 October close of 0.69311 before rebuilding to 0.70331. The 52-week intraday range is 0.64214-0.72804, with spot at the 71st percentile.

bilateral_carry_analysis.carry_regime: Carry favours holding AUD but is too small to drive flows. The CME futures roll premium of -74.2bp a year, against the 72.5bp policy gap, implies a cross-currency basis near zero; the roll combines the interest differential and the basis, and the two cannot be separated without an OIS curve.
bilateral_carry_analysis.breakeven_move: Carry accrues about 4.2 pips a month at spot (0.70331 x 0.725% x 30/365), so over 30 days a long breaks even if spot falls to 0.70289. That cushion is less than a tenth of one ATR (45 pips). Over three months the cushion is about 13 pips and over six months about 26 pips.
bilateral_carry_analysis.carry_assessment: A long AUD/USD position earns +72.5bp a year (RBA 4.60% vs Fed mid-point 3.875%). It would rise to +97.5bp if the RBA hikes on 3 November, and fall back to +72.5bp if the Fed hikes on 9 December. Carry-to-volatility is 72.5bp over 7.228% three-month implied (CME, 98.7-day tenor, observed 29 October) = 0.10. On 60-day realised volatility of 5.89% it is 0.12, and on a 97.5bp gap after a November hike 0.13. All three are far below AUD/CHF (about 0.65) and AUD/JPY (about 0.46). Carry favours holding AUD but is too small to drive flows. The CME futures roll premium of -74.2bp a year roughly matches the policy gap, implying a cross-currency basis near zero. Carry here cannot pay for waiting: a single normal day's range is ten months of carry, so this factor supports the pair's level but cannot justify a standing long on its own.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: The RBA Cash Rate Target of 4.60% sits 72.5bp above the Fed funds mid-point of 3.875%, after the Fed held at 3.75-4.00% on 28 October with two governors dissenting in favour of a hike. Both central banks are tightening, but the RBA moves first. Its 3 November decision is widely expected to take the cash rate to 4.85%, which would widen the gap to 97.5bp, and the Fed's next chance to respond is 9 December, a meeting with new economic projections. Cash-rate futures priced about 78% for 3 November in the latest preview (other reports put it at 85-88%), and all four major Australian banks expect a hike. Fed funds futures price a 9 December hike at about 77%. The rate advantage sits in the front end rather than the long end. The Australian 2-year at 4.93% is 32bp above the US 2-year at 4.61%. The 10-year gap was about +29bp on September monthly averages but only about +16-20bp on late-October closes. Over four weeks the timing favours the pair: the gap widens on 3 November, and the Fed cannot narrow it until 9 December, at the very end of the tactical window. The part of the RBA move that is not yet priced is a small upside risk. Rates feed through to the pair via the 2-year spread and carry demand, but carry is thin against volatility, so the effect is modest.

tactical.what_is_priced: About 20-22bp of the 25bp RBA hike and about 19bp of a 25bp December Fed hike are already priced, so the decision itself offers little edge. The unpriced upside is the RBA's message: if it keeps a tightening bias and pulls a second hike toward the 9 February 2027 decision, that is worth perhaps 10bp on the Australian 2-year.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Over one to three months the policy gap is more likely to round-trip than to trend. A 4.85% cash rate after 3 November and a Fed hike to 4.00-4.25% on 9 December would leave the gap back at 72.5bp, and the RBA's 8 December decision is priced as a hold. The edge lies in what each market prices beyond that. US futures put the funds rate near 4.7% by September 2027, 50-60bp above the Fed's September median projection of 4.1%. Our US view is one more hike and then a hold, so the US path has more room to be priced lower. Australian pricing includes a second RBA hike by around mid-2027, which our Australian view puts only 10-15bp too high given the weakening labour market. If both markets move to those views, the expected one-year differential widens in AUD's favour by roughly 35-45bp. Confidence is low because the risks are close to balanced. Rising Australian unemployment could push RBA pricing toward cuts faster than Fed pricing, and the 9 December Fed projections could back the market rather than the median. The scheduled test of whether the RBA signals a peak is its 9 February 2027 decision.

strategic.what_is_priced: Futures imply AUD depreciating about 0.74% a year against USD, which matches the current differential plus a small basis. We think the US rate path is the more overpriced of the two, a modest AUD-positive mispricing that would be tested at the 9 December Fed projections and the 9 February RBA decision.

factors.horizon_split: Bullish on both horizons, with confidence slipping from 52 to 50. Tactically the RBA hikes first and the Fed cannot respond until 9 December. Strategically the gap is likely to return to 72.5bp, and the bullish case rests only on the US path being more overpriced than Australia's.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: Growth momentum has swung clearly toward the US. US third-quarter GDP grew 3.4% annualised (0.83% q/q), against 0.4% q/q in Australia's June quarter. October flash composite PMIs are 57.6 in the US and 47.7 in Australia, a gap of almost 10 points. Inflation points the other way: Australian monthly CPI is 4.3% and the September-quarter trimmed mean 3.7%, against US core PCE of 3.1% and headline CPI of 3.7%. But Australian inflation is driven by costs (fuel up 9.4% in September, electricity up 12.8% y/y) in an economy whose labour market is cracking. Employment fell 39,300 in September and unemployment rose to 4.7%, the third rise in a row. The US labour market is soft too (payrolls +29,000, unemployment 4.2%), but US activity surveys remain firm. Over four weeks the data calendar is lopsided. US payrolls on 6 November and CPI on 10 November are more likely to confirm the December Fed hike. Australia's October labour force report in the third week of November and the 25 November CPI carry more downside risk for the RBA's 2027 path. These data move the pair through expectations of each central bank's path beyond its next meeting.

tactical.what_is_priced: Hot Australian inflation is already priced into the 3 November hike. The weakening Australian labour market is not, because futures still carry another hike by mid-2027. US strength is largely priced into December Fed odds, so the risk of relative surprises leans against the pair.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Over one to three months, what drives inflation matters more than its level. Australia has the highest headline inflation in the G10 at 4.3%, with falling real wages, a composite PMI in contraction and unemployment rising from 4.5% in July to 4.7% in September. CommBank, which now expects a November hike, also expects weaker growth, softer house prices and higher unemployment as rates bite. That is a stagflationary mix, in which central banks usually stop early. The US is slowing from 3.4% growth but from a much stronger position: ISM manufacturing is 54.5, AI-related investment is holding up, and the Fed projects core PCE easing to 2.5% in 2027. Australia's September-quarter GDP on 2 December, which our Australian view expects at 0.2-0.3% q/q, and the December-quarter CPI on 27 January both feed into the 9 February RBA decision. The growth gap would only close if the US labour market cracks, which is the main risk to this stance. A rise in US unemployment to 4.5% would shift the Fed faster than anything now visible in Australian data.

factors.horizon_split: Bearish on both horizons, with confidence rising from 55 to 58. Over one to three months the cost-driven Australian inflation and three straight rises in unemployment decide how long the RBA can hold, and that weighs more than any single release.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: AUD reacts more strongly than USD to global equities, credit and China, so weaker risk appetite usually lowers the pair. The signals have turned cautious. US investment-grade spreads of 89bp and high-yield spreads of 326bp are at the 95th-96th percentiles of their one-year ranges. The VIX rose from 17.2 to around 20 intraday on 30 October after disappointing technology earnings. China's October manufacturing PMI fell to 49.3. The partial offset is that the dollar is not currently acting as a safe haven: it fell during the 30 October equity sell-off while the yen and franc took the demand. A risk-off episode would therefore hurt AUD mainly through China and commodities rather than help USD through haven buying. The 3 November US midterms cut both ways. A dovish Fed repricing would weaken the dollar, but a return to US trade measures would hit AUD as the most liquid China proxy. Credit Agricole notes that weaker risk appetite could frustrate AUD gains even after a hawkish RBA. On balance, near-term risk leans against the pair.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Over one to three months, risk appetite is genuinely two-sided for this pair. On the bearish side, credit stress, doubts over AI spending and Brent above US$110 could combine into a global slowdown, in which AUD has historically lagged the dollar. On the bullish side, an AI-led equity correction would hit US assets first. Foreign investors hold US equities with low currency hedges, so a correction could push them to sell dollars forward, which weakens USD without any haven bid. Separately, a settlement in the Strait of Hormuz would be a strong positive supply shock for an AUD that is now carrying the oil burden. China's third-quarter GDP of 4.5% y/y and the chance of more stimulus cushion the downside. With the tail risks roughly balanced and the central case a cautious range, this factor gives no strategic signal. A sustained move in US high-yield spreads above 400bp would turn it Bearish; a fall below 280bp would turn it Bullish.

factors.horizon_split: Tactically, the credit warning and the China PMI miss are immediate, and AUD's higher sensitivity to them makes them costly within four weeks. Strategically, those risks are balanced by the hedging channel against USD and by the upside from a Hormuz settlement.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: Positioning on both currencies is tilted against the pair, but the extreme is on the AUD side. In the week to 27 October, asset managers held a net short of 125,237 AUD futures contracts. The legacy non-commercial net short was 128,300, well beyond the -80,000 level that has historically marked AUD extremes, while leveraged funds were net long 48,414 and cutting. On the USD side, leveraged funds are long the dollar against the six major currency futures by about USD 15.9bn. Dollar-index length, though, is at the 83rd-87th percentile of one year and only the 57th-71st of five, so the dollar long is moderate rather than crowded. Taken together, speculators are short the pair, with most of the crowding in AUD. Options agree: the one-month 25-delta risk reversal is -0.97 vols at 35.7 days, so downside protection is already well owned. A near-record short facing a central bank about to hike is fuel for a squeeze if the 3 November decision keeps a tightening bias. The asset-manager short shrank by 3,502 contracts in the latest week, its first reduction since September.

tactical.what_is_priced: Positioning prices a failure of the Australian rate story, even though a hike is 78-88% priced. If the RBA hikes and keeps its tightening bias, covering even a fifth of the asset-manager short would be a meaningful flow in AUD's favour within two weeks.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Over one to three months, positioning still helps the pair, but more as a floor than a reversal signal. The AUD asset-manager short, worth about USD 8.8bn and roughly 39% of open interest, was built as iron ore fell and the current-account deficit hit a record. Those drivers are not reversing quickly, and similar shorts in 2015 and 2019 were held for two to three quarters before being covered. For the pair to keep falling, new sellers are needed. With asset managers near their 25-week extreme and leveraged funds long only 48,414, the next seller is hard to find. On the USD side, slower flows lean against the dollar. Its share of allocated reserves fell to 56.70% in Q2 2026 from 57.18%. Foreign holders of US assets with low hedges have a growing incentive to sell dollars forward as the Fed nears its peak. Japanese real-money demand for Australian bonds, with a wide yield gap over JGBs, is a further slow support. Net, positioning limits the downside more than it creates upside.

strategic.what_is_priced: The market is positioned for a sustained AUD decline driven by terms of trade. Because few sellers are left, we expect any decline to be shallower than this positioning implies, while USD faces slow supply from reserve diversification and rising hedge ratios.

factors.horizon_split: Bullish on both horizons, with confidence falling from 55 to 50. A squeeze needs a trigger, and the 3 November RBA decision is one. Over one to three months the terms-of-trade case behind the short can keep it in place, so positioning cushions the downside rather than driving the pair higher.

tactical.combined_positioning_signal: Speculators are short the pair: an extreme AUD short (legacy non-commercial -128,300, asset managers -125,237) plus a moderate dollar long (leveraged funds about USD 15.9bn across six currency futures). The crowding is concentrated in AUD.
tactical.unwind_trigger: A 25bp RBA hike on 3 November that keeps the commitment to raise rates further if needed, or a negative US payroll print on 6 November that cuts December Fed hike odds below 50%.
tactical.historical_analogue: 2019, when a legacy AUD net short beyond -80,000 contracts was followed by an AUD/USD rally of about 4-5% over the next quarter, once a US-China trade truce provided the trigger.
tactical.contrarian_case: The crowd is short AUD because of iron ore near a two-year low and a record current-account deficit. It is right on those fundamentals but late on positioning. With the RBA about to deliver its fifth hike of the year and the dollar long only moderate, the pain trade is a rise in the pair, and options already price downside protection richly.

strategic.combined_positioning_signal: The AUD short is near its 25-week extreme while dollar length is middling over five years, so the pair's positioning is stretched short but can persist while the terms-of-trade drivers stay in place.
strategic.unwind_trigger: A Hormuz settlement that takes Brent below US$90, or Chinese construction stimulus that lifts iron ore above US$105. Either would remove the fundamental case for the AUD short.
strategic.historical_analogue: 2015 and 2019, when asset-manager AUD shorts built on falling commodity prices were held for two to three quarters before covering, as gradual cushioning rather than a sudden reversal.
strategic.contrarian_case: Over one to three months the crowded short is a floor under the pair rather than a reason to buy it. A forceful unwind needs a fundamental trigger. Without one, covering is likely to be gradual and to soften, not reverse, any drift lower driven by terms of trade and growth.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: Both economies run current-account deficits, but Australia's is wider and getting worse faster. It reached a record A$27.2bn in the June quarter, 3.67% of GDP, against the US deficit of USD 246.0bn, 3.0% of GDP. Terms of trade are moving sharply apart. Iron ore, about 35% of Australian export revenue, traded near US$90.60 a tonne on 26 October after a two-year low near US$89.75. Brent at US$114-118 raises Australia's fuel import bill, while the US, a net energy exporter with cheap domestic gas, gains on its terms of trade. Direct trade adds a small but steady flow in USD's favour: IMF data show Australia exporting $15.7bn of goods to the US and importing $35.6bn in 2024, a $19.9bn bilateral deficit. Within four weeks the only Australian external release is the September trade balance on 5 November, which our Australian view expects to show a surplus below A$2bn. This factor therefore weighs on the pair but carries little tactical weight.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: External balance is the largest strategic drag on the pair. Australia's record June-quarter deficit was built before iron ore fell to a two-year low, so the September-quarter balance of payments on 1 December should be wider still. Iron ore faces structural supply pressure from the Simandou ramp-up and weak Chinese steel demand, and oil stays high while Hormuz shipping is disrupted. The US position is weak too: its net international investment position worsened by USD 1.15tn in one quarter to -USD 22.42tn. But the deficit is easily financed, with USD 300.7bn of net foreign long-term purchases in August, and an oil shock improves US terms of trade against every major importer. Valuation also leans against AUD. The BIS real effective rate is 116.13 for AUD, near the top of its two-year range and 8.77 points higher than a year ago, against 107.11 for USD, at the 21st percentile of its range. In real terms, then, AUD is rich and USD cheap. GDP-based PPP puts the pair only 1.6% below fair value, so PPP itself is neutral. Taken together, a deteriorating Australian external position combined with a rich real exchange rate argues for the pair underperforming over one to three months.

net_commodity_exposure.base_commodity_profile: AUD: a major exporter of iron ore (about 35% of export revenue), coal and LNG, and an exporter of gold. It is a net importer of refined fuel, so high oil prices currently widen the goods deficit even though LNG and coal partly offset that.
net_commodity_exposure.quote_commodity_profile: USD: a net energy exporter of crude, products and LNG, with low domestic gas prices (Henry Hub US$2.76). Higher oil improves US terms of trade relative to energy importers. It has little direct exposure to iron ore.
net_commodity_exposure.net_effect_calculation: Iron ore is the clearest driver. A fall hurts AUD directly and has no meaningful USD offset, so a 10% drop in iron ore is clearly bearish for the pair. Oil is less clear-cut. The framework's default rule gives AUD a mild positive from higher oil, but the current evidence points the other way: Australia's goods and services balance swung to a A$5.1bn deficit on an oil-driven import surge, and higher oil hurts Asian demand for Australian resources. Meanwhile the US, as a net energy exporter, gains. Netting the two legs, higher oil is mildly bearish for the pair in this regime, and lower oil mildly bullish. Gold, which would normally help AUD, fell to a one-year low on 30 October, so it adds nothing.
net_commodity_exposure.scenario_oil_up_10pct: Mildly bearish for the pair. Australia's fuel import bill rises and Asian demand weakens, while US terms of trade improve. A move this size would also lift inflation in both economies, adding to hike pressure at both the RBA and the Fed and largely cancelling out through rates.
net_commodity_exposure.scenario_oil_down_10pct: Mildly bullish for the pair. Australia's terms of trade recover and global growth expectations improve. A drop driven by a Hormuz settlement would be strongly bullish, because it would also improve risk appetite.
net_commodity_exposure.dominant_commodity_driver: Iron ore, through Chinese steel demand and Simandou supply; oil is secondary and currently works against AUD.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: The two central banks are communicating differently. The RBA gives an explicit tightening bias: its 29 September statement committed to raising the cash rate further if needed, after a unanimous 9-0 vote. Deputy Governor Hauser then said the inflation outlook was materially worse than forecast, and Governor Bullock questioned whether four hikes would be enough. The Fed is hawkish in tone, with two dissents for a hike and a statement promising to deliver price stability. But Chair Warsh refuses to give forward guidance outside a crisis and will not pre-judge December, so US signalling is opaque. The order of meetings matters. The RBA speaks first on 3 November, and the Fed's minutes on 18 November are its only scheduled communication in the window before the 9 December decision. Coverage expects a Statement on Monetary Policy alongside the RBA decision, although the verified meeting schedule does not flag it as a projection round. If forecasts are updated, a year-end trimmed-mean forecast lifted toward 3.7% would reinforce the tightening bias. Clear hawkish guidance from one bank against opaque guidance from the other tilts this factor toward the pair over four weeks.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Over one to three months, both banks are likely to turn toward signalling a peak, and both moves would be dovish relative to what markets price. Our Australian view expects the RBA to drop its tightening bias at or before the 9 February 2027 decision as unemployment rises, which would take 10-15bp out of Australian pricing. Our US view expects the 9 December Fed projections to confirm one hike and then a hold, which would challenge a market path some 50-60bp above the Fed's median. The US repricing is potentially larger, but the Fed's refusal to give guidance makes its path less predictable, and the market has sided with the hawkish dissenters. The RBA has rebuilt credibility by following through on four hikes. The Fed has delivered too, but inflation has been above target for nearly six years. Neither bank has a clear credibility advantage, and both pivots point the same way, so this factor is neutral for the pair strategically.

factors.horizon_split: Tactically the RBA's explicit tightening bias faces a Fed that offers no guidance, and the RBA speaks first. Strategically both banks are likely to signal peaks, so their guidance changes broadly cancel out.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: The pair's two biggest events fall on the same day: the RBA decision and the US midterm elections, both on 3 November. Prediction markets put a Democratic House at 94% and a sweep at 70%. Brown Brothers Harriman's base case is that a Democratic House tilts risks toward a dovish Fed repricing and a weaker dollar, which favours the pair. ING warns that a Republican loss of the House could push the administration back toward trade measures, which would hit AUD through China more than it would hurt USD. The Iran war is the second source of risk. Two tankers were struck near Hormuz on 29-30 October, and the President has said the US will not strike before the midterms, leaving the period after them open. A strike would hurt AUD through oil and risk; a ceasefire would help it strongly. Our estimates put a US strike within four weeks at about 15-20% and a ceasefire at about 15%. With the election result largely priced and the oil tails roughly balanced, this factor is neutral tactically.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Over one to three months, geopolitical risk leans slightly against the pair. The base case for the Iran war is that it persists rather than resolves, and each month of disrupted Hormuz transit keeps Brent near US$110, draining Australian national income while improving US terms of trade. US trade policy is a second channel. If a divided Congress pushes the administration toward tariffs, the sign for USD is unclear, but the effect on AUD, the most liquid China proxy, is clearly negative. Against this, US fiscal deadlines add dollar risk: the continuing resolution funding the government expires on 11 December, and a lapse would raise risk premia on US assets. Domestic political risk in Australia is low, with no federal election due before 2028. Our Australian view puts the chances by April 2027 at 25% for a settlement, 25% for escalation and 50% for persistence. Persistence alone is a slow drag on AUD, which tilts this factor marginally bearish.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: Australia's fiscal position is clearly stronger than the US one. Australia ran a 2025-26 deficit of A$22.3bn, 0.8% of GDP, has gross debt of 33.2% of GDP, and is rated AAA by all three agencies (S&P reaffirmed in August). The US ran an FY2026 deficit of USD 2.0tn, 6.2% of GDP, has debt held by the public of about 100% of GDP and interest costs of about 3.4% of GDP, and is rated one notch below AAA with stable outlooks. Within four weeks, though, there is no event likely to make this gap matter for the pair. The US quarterly refunding on 4 November is expected to leave coupon sizes unchanged, and the government funding deadline of 11 December falls just after the tactical window. Australia's Mid-Year Economic and Fiscal Outlook is not due until December. Neither long-end yield shows a sovereign stress premium that is moving the currency. The factor is neutral tactically, with high confidence.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Over one to three months the fiscal gap becomes a modest support for the pair. The US combines a 6.2%-of-GDP deficit outside a recession with interest costs of about a fifth of federal revenue, and a Democratic House from January 2027 makes budget confrontations more likely. Before that, Congress must extend funding that expires on 11 December. The US 30-year at 5.32% and a 10-year real yield of 2.63%, near the top of their five-year ranges, show markets charging a term premium. If that premium rises without a matching rise in policy expectations once the Fed stops hiking, it would weaken rather than support the dollar. Australia's December fiscal update may widen projected deficits by A$5-10bn as iron ore revenue falls. That is not material at a 33% debt ratio, and the AAA ratings are secure. The asymmetry favours AUD, but the US deterioration is gradual and demand for Treasuries remains deep, so confidence is low.

Downside views are cheaper in spot or forwards than in expensive puts, given that carry costs only about 0.06% a month.

The 8 December RBA and 9 December Fed decisions, the latter with projections, sit back to back and are the main strategic repricing points. The 9 February 2027 RBA decision is the scheduled test of a possible RBA peak.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: Dollar liquidity is tightening into year-end, which works against the pair through the USD leg. Reserve balances fell USD 68.8bn in the week to 28 October to a weekly average of USD 2,893.8bn, below the USD 3tn level many treat as the edge of ample. The Treasury's cash balance rose above USD 1tn, well above its USD 850bn end-December target. Balance-sheet runoff has ended, but reserve management purchases have been zero since mid-August, so nothing is offsetting the drain. SOFR printed 3.94% on 29 October, 4bp above interest on reserves, a sign of mild tightness in secured funding. Australian banks raise a meaningful share of their funding in offshore dollar markets, so any year-end widening in dollar funding costs feeds directly into AUD. The CME AUD futures roll premium of -74.2bp a year, against a 72.5bp policy gap, suggests the basis is near zero for now, so the risk is prospective rather than visible. The swap lines (USD 156m) and the standing repo facility are barely used, so this is tightness, not stress. Over four weeks, the direction of travel favours USD.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Over one to three months the funding drag should fade. Treasury plans to run its cash balance down to USD 850bn by end-December, which would return about USD 165bn of reserves from the 28 October level and ease conditions in early 2027. The Fed has a tested tool in reserve management purchases, which ran at USD 40bn and then USD 10bn a month before stopping in mid-August, and its implementation note authorises bill and short-coupon purchases to keep reserves ample. The Fed is therefore likely to respond to any persistent scarcity rather than let funding tighten into the spring. On the dollar smile, liquidity is neither scarce enough to push the dollar to the stressed left side nor abundant enough to push it to the bottom. A December Fed hike would add to dollar yield appeal, but it is largely priced. With tightness likely met by renewed purchases and liquidity returning after year-end, the factor is neutral for the pair strategically.

tactical.score_interpretation: A net score of -0.0262 is Neutral, with a slight bearish lean. It nets two opposing groups of roughly equal size: three AUD-positive factors totalling +0.2183 (policy rates, positioning, guidance) and four AUD-negative factors totalling -0.2445 (growth, liquidity, risk appetite, external balance). No factor has confidence above 55, so the result reflects broad but shallow evidence on both sides rather than one strong driver. The stance is a standoff, not an absence of information. Mapping to conviction: the score lies between -0.10 and +0.10, so the stance is Neutral by rule. Conviction 2 reflects a standoff between two identifiable, dated groups of forces rather than an absence of signal.
tactical.rationale: At tactical weights, Policy & Rates (0.24), Inflation & Growth (0.18) and USD Liquidity (0.11) carry 53% of the score, and they disagree. Rates add +0.1248: the RBA is expected to lift the cash rate to 4.85% on 3 November, widening the gap over the Fed to 97.5bp, and the Fed cannot respond until 9 December. But about 78-88% of that hike is priced. Growth subtracts 0.099, because the US leads Australia by almost 10 points on composite PMIs and Australian unemployment has risen three months running to 4.7%. Liquidity subtracts 0.0605 as US reserves fall below USD 2.9tn into year-end. The net score of -0.0262 is Neutral. The two standalone views interact here: our AUD view is a Neutral with a bullish lean built on the hike, while our USD view is Bullish on growth and funding. In the pair, the rate tailwinds from both sides largely cancel, leaving the growth and funding gap to lean slightly against AUD. The main pair-specific modifier is positioning. A legacy AUD net short of 128,300 contracts against only moderate dollar length means a hawkish RBA could squeeze the pair harder than fundamentals justify, while the dollar's weak haven response blunts the risk-off channel. What is priced is an RBA hike and a December Fed hike. Our edge is that Australian labour data are more likely to disappoint than US activity data, offset by the chance the RBA keeps a tightening bias. The path of least resistance is two-way and event-driven: the RBA decision and US midterms on 3 November, the Australian trade balance on 5 November, US payrolls on 6 November, US CPI on 10 November, the Australian wage index and FOMC minutes on 18 November, the Australian labour force in the third week of November and Australian CPI on 25 November. Conviction is 2: the opposing forces are each credible, so a directional call would rest on which data surprise comes first rather than on a measured imbalance. Conviction would rise if the RBA keeps a conditional tightening bias and positioning starts to cover, or if Australian unemployment reaches 4.9% while US payrolls hold up.
tactical.g10_relative_ranking: Among AUD crosses, AUD/USD offers one of the least attractive risk-adjusted setups. Its carry over volatility of 0.10 trails AUD/CHF and AUD/JPY by a wide margin, and it lacks the clean terms-of-trade divergence of AUD/NOK, which is the cleaner AUD short. Among USD pairs, the dollar's tactical edge is largest against the euro, the yen and the franc. Against AUD it is thin, because AUD carries a higher policy rate and a crowded short. AUD/USD therefore ranks in the middle of the opportunity set: neither the preferred dollar long nor the preferred AUD expression.

strategic.score_interpretation: A net score of +0.0069 is Neutral and almost exactly balanced. The bullish side rests mainly on one low-confidence rates call (+0.12), plus fiscal (+0.0364) and positioning (+0.03). The bearish side is spread across external balance (-0.096), growth (-0.058) and geopolitics (-0.0255). Removing the rates factor alone would turn the score Bearish at about -0.11, so the strategic verdict depends heavily on the judgement that the US rate path is more overpriced than Australia's. Mapping to conviction: the score lies between -0.10 and +0.10, so the stance is Neutral by rule. Conviction is 2.
strategic.rationale: At strategic weights, Policy & Rates (0.24), External Balance (0.16), Guidance (0.12) and USD Liquidity (0.12) dominate. Only two of them carry a signal, and they point in opposite directions. Rates add +0.12. The policy gap should return to 72.5bp after the November RBA and December Fed hikes, but the US market prices a path 50-60bp above the Fed's median projection, while Australian pricing is only 10-15bp too hawkish on our view, so the relative repricing risk favours AUD. External Balance subtracts 0.096. Australia's record A$27.2bn current-account deficit predates iron ore's fall to a two-year low and Brent above US$110, and the BIS real effective rate shows AUD rich (116.13) against a cheap USD (107.11). Growth subtracts 0.058 as Australia's mix of cost-driven inflation and a weakening labour market contrasts with firm US activity. Fiscal (+0.0364) and positioning (+0.03) offset geopolitics (-0.0255). The net +0.0069 is Neutral. The standalone views combine neatly: both our AUD and USD views are Neutral with bearish tilts on their own currencies, which cancel in the pair. The key pair-specific interaction is that both central banks are likely to signal peaks, so guidance nets to zero and the contest becomes a slow external-balance drag on AUD against an overpriced US rate path. Positioning cushions the AUD downside. Bank forecasts range from Westpac and ING at 0.72 to Credit Agricole at 0.69 and CBA at 0.66-0.68, which shows the same lack of consensus. The scheduled tests are the 8 December RBA decision, the 9 December Fed projections, Australia's 1 December balance of payments and 2 December GDP, the 27 January December-quarter CPI and the 9 February 2027 RBA decision. Conviction is 2, not 1, because the forces are identifiable and dated even though they offset. It is not higher because the verdict hinges on one low-confidence rates call. It would turn Bearish if the 9 December projections endorse the market path while Australian unemployment approaches 5%, and Bullish if a Hormuz settlement restores Australia's terms of trade.
strategic.g10_relative_ranking: Strategically, AUD/USD is a low-edge pair. The dollar's weakest strategic legs are against surplus currencies such as the yen, krona and franc, while AUD's weakest are against oil exporters (AUD/NOK, AUD/CAD) and against NZD as the RBNZ tightens. AUD/USD pits two currencies with similar strategic tilts against each other: twin-deficit dollar against terms-of-trade-hit AUD. It ranks behind short AUD/NOK and long AUD/CHF as AUD expressions, and behind short USD/JPY as a dollar-bearish expression.

consensus_divergence.bank_consensus_forecast: There is no tight consensus. Westpac sees AUD/USD at 0.72 in three months (reported 7 October). ING cut its year-end target to 0.72 on 28 September, later raising its short-term target to 0.71 on citing the best volatility-adjusted carry in G10 but expecting a hawkish Fed to cap near-term upside. TD Securities notes about 80% pricing of a November hike limits further AUD support; DBS says AUD has largely priced a 25bp hike. A disclosed aggregate of 24 providers puts the Q4 2026 consensus at 0.71260 (range 0.69000-0.74000) and a March 2027 consensus of 0.7157.

consensus_divergence.our_tactical_view: Neutral (score -0.0262, conviction 2): the RBA hike and crowded AUD short are offset by the US growth lead and tightening year-end dollar funding.
consensus_divergence.our_strategic_view: Neutral (score +0.0069, conviction 2): an overpriced US rate path and a crowded AUD short are offset by Australia's worsening external balance and stagflationary data.
consensus_divergence.divergence_direction: In between: less bullish than Westpac and ING, less bearish than CBA and Credit Agricole's year-end figure.
consensus_divergence.divergence_magnitude: Directional rather than quantified: we do not set a forecast level here. Against the 24-provider Q4 2026 consensus of 0.71260, our probability-weighted end-December path of about 0.7025 is roughly 100 pips below, and our late-April path of about 0.7000 sits below the 0.7157 March provider consensus. Newer bank calls (Credit Agricole 0.69, CBA 0.68, MTFX 0.6900 for December) are 100-225 pips below us.
consensus_divergence.why_we_differ: The bullish banks give more weight to the RBA rate advantage and less to Australia's terms-of-trade loss: iron ore is near a two-year low, Brent is above US$110, and the record current-account deficit came before both moves. They also underweight a labour market where unemployment has risen three months running. The bearish banks, CBA most clearly, underweight positioning: the legacy AUD net short of 128,300 contracts is an extreme that limits further selling. They also underweight the risk that the US rate path, priced 50-60bp above the Fed's median, is cut back. We give both sets of arguments similar weight, and they cancel.
consensus_divergence.payoff_if_right: If the pair stays two-way, outright directional positions on either bank camp's view lose carry and face event volatility for little return. Relative-value and volatility-selling approaches benefit instead.
consensus_divergence.risk_if_wrong: If the bullish camp is right, a Neutral stance misses an RBA-driven short squeeze. If CBA is right, it misses a terms-of-trade-driven decline. The tail where we would be most wrong is a hawkish RBA combined with a weak US payroll print in the first week of November. If the consensus near 0.7126 proves right, a range-fade short from 0.7095-0.7111 is stopped out at 0.7150 for a loss of 39-55 pips. If CBA's 0.68 proves right, the range-fade long at 0.6925-0.6940 is stopped at 0.6865, and the Neutral stance forgoes about 230 pips of downside.

cross_horizon_consistency.explanation: Aligned: tactical Neutral (-0.0262, conviction 2); strategic Neutral (+0.0069, conviction 2). Both horizons are Neutral, but the balance shifts. Tactically, growth momentum and year-end dollar funding slightly outweigh the RBA hike and the crowded AUD short. Strategically, liquidity turns neutral as the Treasury runs down its cash balance and Fed purchases become likely, external balance gains weight, and the rates factor depends on the US path being overpriced. The result is a near-zero score built from larger opposing contributions. Reservation on the settled direction: first, the strategic balance is fragile in a known direction, because one low-confidence rates judgement is the only thing holding it at zero; if the 9 December Fed projections validate the market path, the strategic stance becomes Bearish without any other change. Second, the external-balance and geopolitics factors were scored with Brent at US$114-118. On 2 November, renewed optimism over Iran diplomacy lifted investor confidence and supported the risk-sensitive Aussie, and oil fell sharply. If that holds below US$95, the factors scored bearish on oil would weaken, so the oil invalidator is the one to watch first. The price data says nothing about which way either point will break; it only shows that the pair is coiled and ready to move on whichever arrives first.
cross_horizon_consistency.trading_implication: The fundamentals do not justify a standing directional position on either horizon. The pair should be treated as event-driven around 3 November (RBA and US midterms), the 6 and 10 November US data, and the back-to-back 8-9 December RBA and Fed decisions. Any directional exposure should be small and tied to the outcome of those events. Tactical trade plan: no position at spot; sizing for every idea is half a standard risk unit, set so the stop distance (about 1.0-1.5 ATRs, 45-70 pips) equals 0.25% of capital. (1) Range fade at resistance: sell 0.7095-0.7111, stop 0.7150, target 0.7030. (2) Range fade at support: buy 0.6925-0.6940 above the seven-touch band, stop 0.6865 below its lower edge, target 0.7030. Strategic trade plan: no standing AUD/USD position, half a standard risk unit per idea. (1) Sell rallies into the four-touch 0.7167-0.7231 band, stop 0.7290 (above the 52-week high), target 0.7030. (2) Buy dips into 0.6880-0.6920, stop 0.6820, target 0.7030. (3) Re-assess both legs after the 9 December Fed projections and the 9 February RBA decision. Directional strategic risk is better held in the crosses the ranking favours (short AUD/NOK, long AUD/CHF) or in short USD/JPY.

assumptions: Price data: the analysis uses daily closing prices for AUD/USD over 130 weekday sessions from 2026-05-04 to 2026-10-30, which covers the six-month strategic horizon. Spot is 0.70331 at the 30 October close. The valuation date of 1 November is a Sunday, so the gap between spot and valuation is one weekend. Every level, pip distance and percentage is computed against that spot. Commentary from 2 November is used only qualitatively, never as a substitute price. No weekend bars were present or removed.

Averages, zones and history: the moving averages, the 200-week average and the support and resistance zones are computed over the full stored history of 4,920 weekday sessions from 2007-12-24 to 2026-10-30 (1,011 weekly and 502 monthly bars). Moving averages are simple averages of trading-day closes. Realised volatility is annualised on 252 trading days. ATR is the 14-day average true range.

Data-quality notes: only 2 resistance zones and 9 support zones met the two-touch threshold. The resistance list is therefore supplemented with the 52-week intraday high (0.72804) and round numbers (0.7300, 0.7500), marked as supplementary. Zone distances are quoted to each band's midpoint and its nearest edge.

Rates: policy rates are the RBA Cash Rate Target of 4.60% (as of 29 October) and the Fed funds mid-point of 3.875% (as of 27 October). The 10-year yields in the rate data are September monthly averages (5.283% and 4.99%, a +29.3bp gap) and are not quoted as live levels. Late-October closes of about +16-20bp are used for the current gap.

Options and funding: implied volatilities and risk reversals are CME at-the-money AUD/USD futures-option values observed 29 October. The three-month tenor is 98.7 days, not 90, because CME lists quarterly expiries. No one-year implied history exists, so the implied level is placed within the six-month range of 20-day realised volatility instead of being given a percentile. Forward points are derived from the CME futures roll premium of -74.2bp a year, which combines the interest differential and the cross-currency basis and cannot be separated without an OIS curve. No published option-barrier levels for this pair were found.

Scenarios: scenario targets are anchored to the computed zones. Probability-weighted outcomes use 50/25/25 weights. Standard-deviation comparisons use implied volatility scaled to the 35.7-day and 189.6-day tenors.

Bilateral trade: goods trade uses IMF Direction of Trade Statistics for 2024, as reported by Australia: exports to the US $15.7bn, imports $35.6bn, net -$19.9bn. The US-reported mirror figures (US exports to Australia $34.6bn, imports $16.7bn) differ by about $1bn on each side, which is normal mirror-statistics asymmetry.
